  • Sitting at a picnic table in the shade, I pulled up my blog.
  • I picked at my leftover Chinese food for breakfast as I sorted through my resupply and packed my backpack for the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I packed up from my stealth spot before daybreak and used the park bathroom to change and brush my teeth.

Sitting at a picnic table in the shade, I pulled up my blog. That’s when I realized I had forgotten to hit publish on the post I had scheduled for the previous week. I rushed to get it published, feeling frustrated with myself and the growing pressure to keep up with my writing. Once my blog was published online, I spent the remainder of the morning working on my next entry.

I picked at my leftover Chinese food for breakfast as I sorted through my resupply and packed my backpack for the trail.

Walking through town, I stopped at Carl’s Jr. for a Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese and a strawberry milkshake. I packed the burger away to eat later on the trail.

Before hitching out, I stopped at Elevation Gear, where I finished my ice cream and spent a few minutes visiting with Marble, Electrolyte, and Pickles while telling them my plans.

Industry observers note that walking along the road toward the Horseshoe Meadow turnoff, I dropped my pack to hitch. I stood with my thumb out, hoping for a ride. A few vehicles stopped to offer rides, but they were heading either to Whitney Portal or the Alabama Hills. A couple of other drivers pulled over only to tell me they didn’t have room.

The gestures were kind, but each time a vehicle stopped, my hopes went up. Having them dashed by another apology made the wait even more discouraging.

After 30 minutes with no luck, I grabbed my backpack and walked farther out of town.

A farmer working in a field across the street told me he had been watching me try to hitch a ride down the road. He wished me luck.

“The right ride will come.” I told him.

Five minutes later, a car pulled over.

The driver, Taquito, told me he was a Triple Crown thru-hiker from Omaha. He was on vacation, hiking and providing trail magic to hikers. We talked about hiking, his Triple Crown experiences, and the trail magic he was sharing with hikers. He took me all the way to the Horseshoe Meadow trailhead.

In a recent development, at the trailhead, Taquito offered me even more trail magic in the form of Gatorade, an apple, and Gummy Clusters. Taking advantage of the nearby trash cans, I drank the Gatorade, ate the apple, and demolished my double burger before heading out on the trail. I tucked the Gummy Clusters away for later.

Industry observers note that leaving the trailhead at 4:30 p.m., I began my hike into the mountains. Lone Pine had been hot during the day, now, in elevation the evening air was getting cold. The loose, sandy trail made walking difficult, especially with my heavy backpack. I moved slowly, tired and a little stressed about finding a place to camp before the elevation started.

It has been revealed that I spent too much time looking off-trail for flat spots. Two miles in, the trees began to grow thicker, I suddenly came across a sandy clearing with a rabbit. Seeing it hopping around so carefree made the area feel safe and inviting. I liked the idea of sharing this little clearing with the rabbit, so I decided this was where I would camp.

I used my newly acquired ice axe to scrape and level the sandy ground, making a flat spot for my tent.

Sources indicate that for dinner, I made a Frito taco bowl with dehydrated pea-protein “beef” and dried refried beans. It hit the spot after a long day. With a full belly, a newly leveled tent spot, and a rabbit for company, I crawled into my tent. Too tired to write, I fell asleep around 8 p.m. with a bit of daylight still lingering. I had a long way to go, but at least I was back in the mountains.

In a recent development, I woke up at 3 a.m. to a dark, chilly morning. I was camped on the Cottonwood Pass Trail, 2.6 miles from its junction with the PCT at Mile 751.4. Nearly 1,200 feet lower in elevation. I opened one of my tent vestibules to help ventilate the condensation before burrowing back into my quilt for a little more rest.

At 4:15 a.m., I woke to the howling of coyotes. It made me smile. I love being in nature. Still tucked into my quilt, I reached for my headlamp in the top pocket of my backpack, where I always keep it. Although I normally sleep with it around my neck, I knew exactly where to find it.

While getting breakfast ready, I also pulled out my snacks for the day. I try to eat my heavier, bulkier foods first to lighten my pack. As I was packing up, I spotted Spicy Bite (Southern California) hiking toward town. He graciously offered to carry out my trash. Everything was inside a Ziploc bag, including half a family-size bag of Fritos that I had hiked in. I slipped the bag into his backpack without making him take it off. One less thing to carry!

It has been revealed that A little after 7 a.m., I was hiking across a green, grassy meadow covered in frost. The sun hadn’t yet risen over the mountains, and the air grew colder as I approached a stream. After crossing it, I looked up at the steep mountainside ahead. I checked my map, trying to figure out where the trail passed through the snow-covered pass above. I began preparing myself for the climb.

The trail entered a pine forest and began to switchback.

Sources indicate that the sun began to warm the earth. Chipmunks scurried over the white boulders and fallen logs along the trail. At the last switchback before the top, I stopped for a break. I was above 11,000 feet and beginning to notice a slight headache coming on. After five minutes, I pushed on to the top and finally rejoined the PCT.

Sources indicate that just minutes later, I stopped at the first trickle of flowing water. My headache was slowly developing, and my stomach wasn’t feeling right. I needed to hydrate and give myself time to adjust before continuing farther into the Sierras. I spent the next hour and a half sitting beside the trail at 11,132 feet, drinking water and trying to stay warm. My headache improved slightly, but I still wasn’t feeling quite right.

It has been revealed that pushing to higher elevations can be dangerous. In 2022, I had been just a few days behind a young hiker who lost her life on Forester Pass due to altitude-related challenges. That experience had stayed with me and reminded me not to take the mountains lightly.

As I packed up, I noticed another hiker continuing past the Lone Pine exit. It was Diva (Tennessee), who had already built up his trail legs after hiking the Appalachian Trail and then the Florida Trail over the past year. He was planning to continue north to Kearsarge Pass.

We hiked together to the frozen Chicken Spring Lake, where we met a group of local high school students and their teachers. The students were about to graduate and were on a 20-day backpacking trip.

Having organization lifted my spirits, even though I still wasn’t feeling 100%. Before leaving the lake, I noticed my feet were feeling swollen and my shoes were getting tight. With the altitude already on my mind, it was another thing I was paying attention to. I took an ibuprofen, collected a little more water, and said goodbye as Diva continued north.

Sources indicate that as I climbed over the next pass and entered Kings Canyon National Park, the landscape opened up to beautiful views. A meadow stretched out to my left, while the trail wrapped around the mountainside. To my right, the majestic pink and white rock walls of Cirque Peak towered above me at 12,900 feet.

Recent findings suggest that I stopped for lunch and noticed dark clouds gathering in the distance. I moved more snacks into my hip-belt pocket. With most of my elevation gain behind me for the day, I wasn’t too concerned about being caught in a storm while exposed on a climb, though I did pick up my pace.

It has been revealed that as thunder rumbled in the dark clouds, I hurried to the next water source. I found a few flat spots nearby and collected water, letting my gravity filter do its work while I set up my tent. With the storm moving in, I wanted to get settled before it arrived.

Industry observers note that happy with my setup, I was about to put my gear inside when I looked up. Above my tent, I saw one dead tree leaning against another, with yet another dead tree on the opposite side. With thunder sounding closer, I quickly decided to move my tent. I relocated to a completely different spot a short distance away.

In a recent development, another hiker, Scott (New Zealand), came down the trail. He was planning to continue a few more miles before setting up for the night. I finally threw my gear into my tent just as it started to hail.

Small hailstones continued falling steadily. I occasionally bumped the sides of my tent to knock off the accumulating ice. It was only 5 p.m., but I was happy to be inside and dry, with enough water for the night.

I boiled water and mixed half a Mountain House pepperoni pizza meal with half a chicken alfredo meal.

Sources indicate that after the hail stopped, the golden sun came streaming through the pine trees. Tiny white pieces of hail were scattered across the ground, contrasting with the beautiful green landscape.

I brushed my teeth and placed my bear can behind a large fallen tree as the sun dipped below the mountains.

Crawling into my tent, I thought about how far I had come. I was proud of myself for making it this far on the trail and stepping into the high-altitude Sierras. It had taken bravery and strength to venture this far into the wilderness on my own. Even with the cold, I was genuinely happy to be surrounded by such a beautiful place. I felt grateful to be there, with a deep respect for the mountains and the wilderness I am fortunate enough to experience.

Sources indicate that at 3:45 a.m., my alarm pulled me out of sleep. I wanted to eat up any food that required cooking today so that tomorrow, when I pushed over Forrester Pass, I could just grab bars and snacks and keep moving.

After boiling water, I made oatmeal and a mix of hot cocoa and coffee.

In a recent development, part of the reason I struggle to hike with others is that I’m a slower hiker and take longer to get out of camp. I get frustrated when I’m the last one to leave, and that frustration can often affect my attitude throughout the day.

In a recent development, this morning, I realized that taking my time getting out of camp was a form of self-care. When I give myself time to get everything done without rushing, I’m happier and more relaxed. I also know I’ve taken care of everything at camp and haven’t forgotten any chores.

According to recent reports, at 7 a.m., I continued my hike. The trail descended toward Rock Creek, where it opened into a beautiful grassy valley surrounded by snow-covered mountains. Water was flowing everywhere. It was a completely different landscape from the desert I’d been hiking through the past two months.

As I approached Rock Creek, I passed established campsites, a few with hikers still packing up. The creek was rushing, and the morning air was cold.

Industry observers note that the stepping stones used later in the year were covered in inches of rushing water. Looking downstream, I spotted an old fallen tree with no bark. It would likely be slippery with the frost that morning. A little farther down, I saw a newer-looking fallen tree across the creek. Thinking this might be an option, I started climbing onto it, but some of the bark slipped off, revealing a smooth, slippery surface. Looking farther along the log, I noticed more sections where the bark was missing.

In a recent development, I hiked back upstream, past the trail, but didn’t find any better options for a dry crossing. I felt most comfortable getting my shoes wet, hoping that if I crossed on the rocks, I could at least keep the rest of my clothing dry.

I tried stepping across the rocks first. As soon as both feet were on the slippery rocks, I decided it would be better to just cross the creek. Plunging my legs into the freezing current, the water reached my knees. Even part of my rolled-up pants got wet as I climbed out on the other side.

I met a NOBO JMT hiker named Will (California), who had taken off his shoes to cross the creek and was putting them back on.

At the top of the next hill, I took a break on a boulder with a view, dreaming of French toast with syrup, maybe even peanut butter.

In a recent development, scott from the day before walked up while I was taking a break. This was when we officially met.

Hiking through a rocky boulder field, I heard black-capped Chickadees chirping something that sounded like the word “cheeseburger.” Every time I heard it, I couldn’t help but laugh and found myself getting hungry!

Industry observers note that reaching Crabtree Meadow, I crossed Whitney Creek using a log. I felt a little uneasy about my balance with my backpack and how high the log was above the creek, but I made it across. I was proud of myself!

After crossing Whitney Creek, I passed the first trail junction leading to Mount Whitney.

Recent findings suggest that the PCT climbed through exposed switchbacks with some great views. I stopped halfway up to apply sunscreen.

Passing the second junction to Whitney, I was slightly tempted to take it, but continued hiking the PCT. I didn’t have enough food to add the extra day and a half, and the last forecast I’d read was predicting snow in a few days.

Sources indicate that I picked my way through some patchy snow before arriving at Wallace Creek. After hiking up and down the creek looking for a dry crossing, I couldn’t find one. This time I took off my shoes, socks, calf compression sleeves, and gaiters before crossing.

The creek was cold, the rocks were slippery, and the water was high enough to get the bottom of my shorts a little wet.

I dried my feet with a bandanna and let them air out for a bit before putting everything back on.

It has been revealed that clouds started rolling in as the afternoon continued. I needed to push to get as close to Forrester Pass as I could.

It has been revealed that as I approached the climb up Major Horn Plateau, the clouds grew closer, and I could hear thunder rumbling. Seeing a cluster of trees about 300 feet off the trail, I crossed a small creek to take a break, eat a snack, and assess the storm.

With a snack in my stomach, most of the dark clouds had moved off to the south, though I could still hear thunder rumbling in the distance. I ventured back to the trail, still cautious as I headed toward a treeless area at 11,056 feet, with a metal bear canister in my backpack.

As I climbed onto Substantial Horn Plateau, it began to snow. The clouds obscured some of the panoramic views of the Sierra mountains, though I could still see much of the surrounding landscape. I was exhausted and cold, and I wasn’t particularly happy about being out there in the weather. But stopping wasn’t even a consideration.

My last obstacle for the day was Tyndall Creek. One of the trail notes mentioned a more manageable crossing about a half-mile upstream. As I started heading upstream, a hiker on the other side spotted me and came down to the creek.

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t see him right away and couldn’t hear him over the rushing water. He pointed toward the spot where the trail crossed and told me to just cross there.

Again, I took off my shoes, socks, gaiters, and calf compression sleeves before stepping into the frigid water.

There were a few small groups of hikers scattered among the campsites. I found a semi-flat, semi-secluded spot and set up camp. I made dinner and got ready for bed. Tomorrow was going to be an early start. I was a little nervous about Forrester Pass. I had 5 miles to the top and didn’t want to be plunge-stepping down the north side in the afternoon. I was glad I wouldn’t have to cross Tyndall Creek in the morning.

At 3:00 a.m., I woke to bright stars in the cold morning sky. I mixed coffee into cold water and packed snacks into my pockets. After packing up camp, I took off my puffy and hit the trail at 4:40 a.m.

Recent findings suggest that hiking in the early morning light, I didn’t need my headlamp. The colors in the sky were stunning.

According to recent reports, the trail crossed small snowmelt creeks, weaving in and out of stream crossings. At one point, the melting snow had created a stream right across the trail.

Sources indicate that my feet crunched over the frozen ground, and I slipped a bit on a patch of ice. I realized I needed to be more careful crossing snow bridges, especially with rushing water underneath.

The only person I saw that morning was Scott, who passed me. I was still hoping to find a hiking buddy for the pass, and I was glad everything was so frozen.

As I continued climbing, I kick-stepped up increasingly steep icy fields, trying to avoid the boulders that were beginning to melt and weaken the snow in the morning sun.

As I looked up in awe at 13,897-foot Junction Peak next to it, Forrester Pass, at 13,120 feet, loomed ahead like a boss. I could see two people crossing over its scary icy chute above.

Just then, I heard someone hiking on the ice behind me. I was surprised to see Scott again. He had taken a break off trail, and I must have passed him at some point.

Industry observers note that I told Scott we should hike together up and over the pass, and he agreed. I’m sure he did it just so I would feel more comfortable hiking it. Once we were out of the valley bowl, the switchbacks were mostly clear. They received afternoon sun each day.

In a recent development, as I made my way toward Forrester Pass, I felt a mix of intimidation and excitement. The climb ahead was daunting, and the icy terrain made me nervous, especially the chute. I was more worried about crossing the chute than the north side, although it would turn out that I probably should have been more concerned about the other side. Still, I felt confident in my ability to tackle the challenge. Reaching Forrester Pass would be a huge milestone, both physically and personally. It was the highest point on the PCT, and I was excited to see what it would take to get there.

When we finally reached the ice chute, I watched Scott scoot across the iced-over, foot-shaped holes in the ice. I questioned whether I should take the time to put on my microspikes. I hadn’t worn them yet on the trail.

My heart started to race. I secured my microspikes to the bottom of each shoe and exchanged one of my trekking poles for my ice axe. I crossed the ice chute one foot at a time, never looking down and maintaining three points of contact. Just like that, I was on the rocky trail on the other side.

It has been revealed that thrilled to be over the ice chute, I hollered down into the valley below. Just a few more switchbacks to the highest point on the PCT!

According to recent reports, as I attempted to take a drink of my coffee, I discovered that the liquid around the lid had frozen, and there were chunks of ice inside the bottle. Thirsty as I was, I laughed. How often do you get a frozen coffee with a view like this?

As I crested the pinnacle of the PCT, Forrester Pass, I hollered at the top of my lungs in excitement. We stopped to take in the view and take photos on the blisteringly cold pass. Afterward, we decided it was too icy to glissade, so we would hike down instead. There was more snow on the north side because it received less sunlight during the early spring months. I was glad I had my microspikes. Scott didn’t have any.

Sources indicate that unable to see the trail, we followed footprints as we switchbacked down the ridge, eventually ending up farther out than we should have. Unaware that we were that far off trail, I told Scott I would probably be fine from there, and he picked up his pace.

Sources indicate that following the footprints, we ended up at the edge of the ridge. Scott climbed down over the snow and rocks and continued on. Dark, foggy clouds began rolling in. I hesitated, wondering whether I should backtrack alone to look for the trail or attempt to follow him. I was still reluctant to use my ice axe.

Sources indicate that just then, Scott slipped and slid, landing in a pile of rocks. He yelled out that he was hurt.

It has been revealed that thankfully, Yak and Gezelle were already below us and rushed over to help. I tossed them my first-aid kit.

I decided it was unsafe to try to climb down with my heavy, off-balance backpack, so I took it off and lowered it down using my bear line.

By the time I safely reached the bottom, Scott had already continued hiking on his own. The girls were packing up the first-aid kit and shouldering their packs as two young hikers who had just glissaded down the pass hiked toward us.

Industry observers note that they had been hiking with the girls and were fast hikers. We were really concerned about Scott, even though he had an SOS button. The guys hiked ahead to try to catch up with him.

The three of us women continued hiking downhill, passing stunning teal-blue alpine lakes and crossing streams alongside the roaring Bubbs Creek. We were surrounded by some of the most epic views of beautiful white granite peaks.

Sources indicate that at Mile 784, at an elevation of 10,961 feet, I took off my microspikes. Eventually, most of the snow was gone, replaced by puddles along the rocky trail and the occasional large snowdrift that I had to plunge-step through.

Below 10,000 feet and back in the trees, the girls stopped for a break while I continued hiking. When I reached Bubbs Creek, I noticed a downed tree upstream. I decided to take my shoes off and wade across instead. Waterfalls cascaded everywhere, and the creek was rushing with so much water. Along the trail, I also spotted a young buck.

two guys from earlier, who were taking a break on the side of the trail. They told me Scott was still alive and hadn’t bled out. This was where they had caught up to him, and he was still hiking at a good clip. I was happy to hear the news and relieved that he was doing okay.

In a recent development, with my early start, my quilt had some condensation on it when I packed up. I considered stopping to dry it out, but noticed a cooler breeze and clouds starting to roll in from the west. I wondered if we might get some precipitation.

I continued down the switchbacks toward Vidette Meadow. I was exhausted by the time I reached the trail junction, where there was a bear box. I found a spot a little farther off the trail and set up my tent around 12:30 p.m.

It has been revealed that I collected water and filtered 1.75 liters. After making my Chicken and Vegetable Rice Mountain House meal and having cocoa coffee, I settled in for a nap from 1:00–2:30 p.m. While I napped, my body heat helped dry the condensation from my quilt.

In a recent development, after waking, I decided to stay at the lower elevation rather than climb higher because the weather was uncertain. I spent the afternoon blogging and relaxing at camp. I was almost out of food, and after eating a substantial lunch, I settled for some candy and made tea. Around 7 p.m., I fell asleep again.

At 11:30 p.m., I woke to the sound of precipitation hitting my tent. It was barely sleeting. I checked the tension on my tent, then curled back into my quilt.

Recent findings suggest that in the morning, my tent was covered in a very thin layer of sleet that had slightly melted on contact and stuck to the tent. One guyline had slipped out of place, and a corner of the tent was sagging under the weight. The ground was dusted with tiny sleet pellets and snow.

Before putting on my shoes, I slipped a twist-tie snack bag over each foot. If my feet got wet in these temperatures, I might have trouble keeping them warm. I wanted to do everything I could to keep them dry.

Around 7:00 a.m., I left camp, making fresh tracks on the trail.

Not long after starting, I arrived at a wide stream feeding into the roaring Bubbs Creek. I picked my way across its multiple channels, stepping on fallen logs and large rocks while using my trekking poles for balance.

Industry observers note that I arrived at a trail junction, turned right, and began climbing out of the canyon. As I gained elevation, the trees began to thin, and the terrain gave way to solid rock. As I switchbacked across the cliffs, I had a beautiful view of Kings Canyon and could see the valley I had hiked down the day before. Forrester Pass itself was hidden behind a mountain.

The Kearsarge Pinnacles, along with East and West Vidette Mountains, towered over the valley, dusted with snow. The scenery was so beautiful that it hardly looked real, with every detail highlighted by the white snow.

Industry observers note that crossing flowing streams and seasonal snowmelt, I was glad I had put the bags over my feet that morning. My shoes got damp, but my feet stayed dry and warm.

According to recent reports, there was a brief relief from the climbing as I passed the first trail junction toward Bullfrog Lake and Kearsarge Pass. The plateau was flat and sandy, with a few scattered pine trees. I could see unfamiliar mountains towering in the distance and hear what sounded like military jets booming overhead, though I couldn’t see a single one.

Recent findings suggest that I took the second trail junction, adding 7.6 bonus miles up and over Kearsarge Pass to the trailhead. As I climbed, the trees became increasingly sparse. Near the cutoff leading back down to Bullfrog Lake, I noticed a ranger’s note posted on a rock. It was titled “Bear Info” and warned hikers that bears in the area had gotten food from people and would continue trying to get more. It reminded hikers never to leave food unattended and to keep all food and scented items secured.

The note also included some rather unusual advice about what to do if you encountered a bear!

At 10:00 a.m., I reached Kearsarge Pass at 11,760 feet after hiking five miles and gaining 2,200 feet in elevation.

Inside the Sierras, the skies were partly cloudy with patches of blue. On the Highway 395 side, the sky was cloudy and gray, and I could see a storm blowing in from the north. I was relieved that I had beaten the storm to the pass.

I met a hiker named Crush who was hiking back over the pass. Just then, it started to lightly snow, and it continued throughout the rest of my hike. I was cold as I began the long switchbacks down toward Onion Valley. Major Pothole Lake was covered in ice, its surface a deep blue. On the other side of the lake, three people were practicing self-arresting with their ice axes on the snow.

It has been revealed that passing Gilbert Lake, I noticed patches of green grass and scattered trees around the partially frozen lake. The three men I’d seen practicing with their ice axes passed me on the trail. I was too shy to ask for a ride, thinking they would be long gone by the time I reached the trailhead.

Sources indicate that as the trail continued downhill, I had views of waterfalls cascading down the steep valley walls. In the final mile, the parking lot came into view. I could still see the three men, so I picked up my pace, hoping they were still at the trailhead. If they were, I was going to ask for a ride.

According to recent reports, when I reached the parking lot, I hurried over to where the three men were sitting in their vehicles with the windows down. Thankfully, they had been waiting for me!

Frank and his sons had permits for Mount Whitney on Friday, weather permitting, and had been practicing with their ice axes at elevation. They were heading to Lone Pine in their two vehicles and offered me a ride.

I stopped at the post office in Lone Pine to pick up my newly introduced base layer. Frank and his sons then dropped me a few blocks away at the gear store, where I repacked my backpack.

Recent findings suggest that I was hoping to get a bunk at The Hostel California in Bishop. The hostel was first come, first served, and with cellphone service issues in the area since the windstorm back at Kennedy Meadows South, I wasn’t able to secure a spot ahead of time.

I hiked to the north edge of town and stuck out my thumb, hoping to catch a ride toward Bishop.

Someone pulled over, but they were only going as far as Independence. I thanked them but decided to hold out for a ride all the way to Bishop.

Sources indicate that mark, from Tehachapi, picked me up. He was heading past Bishop to retrieve his family’s RV at June Lake. His family had been camping there with their trailer when they decided to drive into Yosemite the previous day. It ended up snowing, and Tioga Road closed, leaving them unable to get back to their trailer. They had to drive home to Tehachapi, and Mark was now making the trip back to retrieve the RV.As we approached Bishop, I called The Hostel California to check for a bunk. Unfortunately, they were full. Not sure where to go that wouldn’t cost me over three bills, I asked Mark to drop me off at Smart & Final.

It has been revealed that I picked up a bagged salad, a pint of ice cream, a gallon of milk, and a box of cereal for dinner and breakfast. Then I started walking down the snowy streets of Bishop.

Industry observers note that hotel prices were high because the Mule Days festival had just taken place. Heartbroken that the hostel was full and unsure whether I knew any other hikers in town, I started walking down the snowy main street, going from motel to motel asking for a hiker discount.

Sources indicate that by my third stop, I was struggling to hold back tears. If only I knew someone in town I could split a room with. The snowy weather had left the streets nearly empty.

According to recent reports, after leaving my fourth motel, I was considering stealth camping when an angel named Erine pulled over. She had seen me at the store earlier and noticed me wandering down the street. She was a local teacher.

She asked where I was headed. Not really sure myself, I explained that I was looking for a motel that might offer a discount for hikers.

When we arrived at the motel, Erine, the angel of a woman, paid for my room. She also made sure I got my backpack and groceries inside quickly because of the precipitation.

Sources indicate that before leaving, she gave me her phone number in case I needed anything while I was in Bishop and gave me a hug. Then she was gone.

After taking a shower and doing some laundry, I spiderwebbed my bear line around the room. There weren’t many good places to tie it off, but I managed to create a makeshift clothesline.

I spent some time blogging before eating half the salad for dinner. I also brushed the caps of my two Smartwater bottles, which I had been carrying since Mexico. It’s a chore I try to do in every town.

I fell asleep in a soft, warm bed with the TV on.

The skies had cleared up in town. You could still see fresh snow covering the mountains, with clouds beginning to move back over them. I spent my morning eating cereal, drinking coffee, and blogging. It felt good to have time to catch up without feeling so rushed and to have a little less stress on my shoulders.

I received a group message and found out that Google was in town staying at the Motel 6. He offered to split his bed with me for the night.

When checkout time came, I walked down the road with my backpack to the Motel 6. Google and two other hikers had been there for days, and their gear was scattered around the room. I threw my backpack in a corner away from everyone else’s gear.

Recent findings suggest that there was a group wanting to go to Keough’s Hot Springs outside of town. I was unsure if I wanted to go, still having chores to do before leaving town. With snow still predicted in the mountains that day, I had no excuse not to go.

With no rideshares available, we started walking down the road and eventually found a hitch who even offered to take us the few miles off the main road to the hot springs.

Once there, we entered the bathhouse. There was a large, warm pool for swimming and a smaller, hot, shallow pool for soaking. The warm pool had no roof, offering a glimpse of the surrounding scenery. Dark storm clouds hung over the Sierra peaks, making being in the warm water feel even better.

After spending a few hours at the pool, most of it soaking in the hot water and enjoying a pretzel Google shared with me, the group walked the mile back to Highway 395 to hitch a ride to Bishop.

The storm had given the desert valley a beautiful, moody feel, with clouds draped over the White Mountains in front of us.

In a recent development, after returning to the motel with my resupply box, I set it aside to deal with tomorrow. I still hadn’t decided how many days of food I would need for the next stretch. With several challenging mountain passes ahead, I wanted to take some time to make sure I was prepared for what was coming. I spent the rest of the evening relaxing in the room while the others headed out for pub trivia and bowling. It was nice to have a quiet evening before heading back into the mountains.

Industry observers note that 🌈 Welcome to Crispy Hiker! 🥾 Hey there! I'm Crispy, a passionate hiker, free spirit, and outdoor adventurer who believes the best stories are found out on the trail. ☀️ Since 2018, I've explored long-distance trails across the country, from the Pacific Crest Trail ⛰️ to the Appalachian Trail 🌿, along with the Pinhoti Trail, Benton MacKaye Trail, Pine Mountain Trail, and many others. My hiking journey has taken me through mountains 🏔️, forests 🌲, islands 🏝️, and some of the most beautiful landscapes along the way. Each trail brings newly introduced challenges 💪, unforgettable experiences ✨, amazing people, and lessons that stay with me long after the miles are behind me. Through Crispy Hiker, I share my adventures, trail stories, and the real ups and downs of life on the trail. It's about more than reaching a destination. #216992. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1308 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing latest route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • It has been revealed that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing latest route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

It has been revealed that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin stated. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” noted Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he stated.

According to recent reports, there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

Industry observers note that the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

It has been revealed that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Recent findings suggest that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson noted. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

It has been revealed that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” mentioned Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Sources indicate that that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

It has been revealed that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

It has been revealed that once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the major cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

According to recent reports, conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Industry observers note that marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

According to recent reports, in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

It has been revealed that “That is why it is notable to consider all options and potential complications before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

In a recent development, asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they stated. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

In a recent development, they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing swiftly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles mentioned. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

In a recent development, the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they stated.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Recent findings suggest that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

Recent findings suggest that the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • Industry observers note that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

Industry observers note that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Sources indicate that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed plan.

Recent findings suggest that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Industry observers note that keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

It has been revealed that at the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

Sources indicate that today’s post is a brief memo covering my emotions heading into my final 4 day hiking stint. Mostly I am praying I don’t forget anything!

In a recent development, it was difficult to write up the posts from the last two days. The problem was two-fold. Nerves for the upcoming 4 days on trail and ensuring I had thought of everything so I could attempt the 4 state challenge on Sunday. It would be easy to forget a single thing, like my power bank which I rarely take with me. I was also trying to give myself a mental break, but writing the blog posts takes mental energy, so I was battling a catch-22.

The latest weather outlook looks almost too promising to be true. It looks like it will be reaching 60 degrees each of the upcoming 4 days. Overnight lows are hovering around 40 degrees. That would be a miracle given the time of year. Sunday does look cloudy, so catching the sunset at Pen Mar park might fall a bit flat, but if I am successful with my 4 state challenge attempt nothing will be able to dull the ceremony.

In a recent development, perhaps the only item of note is that I have been unable to restock my whole milk powder, all the stores in the area have run out and there seems to be a supply glitch. I am making a proposal to replace my usual breakfast and dinner with something else, probably granola bars and beef sticks. Not ideal, but hopefully a minor change that I can negotiate without impacting my 4 state challenge attempt.

Recent findings suggest that I’ll wrap up the post here, its only been two days since my last zero. There isn’t anything to report that you haven’t read at least a few times already.

Hopefully the butterflies in my stomach are more due to the 3 cups of coffee rather than actual nerves that will seep over into my hiking time tomorrow.

#216986. Latest Update: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Industry observers note that gribbin debuted his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Industry observers note that gribbin debuted his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Recent findings suggest that given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

It has been revealed that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Sources indicate that northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

According to recent reports, the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line highlights the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

It has been revealed that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Recent findings suggest that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with newly introduced designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

According to recent reports, safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Sources indicate that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

In a recent development, successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

Recent findings suggest that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

Industry observers note that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

Industry observers note that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

Industry observers note that the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

Every year, thousands of hikers set out on this unforgettable journey, pushing their limits both physically and mentally as they navigate this incredibly diverse terrain.

In a recent development, this year, wildfires devastated many thru-hikers’ plans. In July, the northern section of the PCT from Harts Pass to the Canadian border was closed due to the Ptarmigan Fire. Because of this, many finish photos look different than in years past.

Sources indicate that thru-hiking teaches lessons in perseverance and resilience, and many hikers were able to pivot from a traditional finish and found creative conclusions to their multi-month journey before the northern terminus officially reopened in mid-September. We’re thrilled to spotlight the incredible hikers who completed this journey in 2026, no matter the end point!

Same Clothes, New Country- Camino Day 49

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I woke up around 6:30 AM, and since breakfast wasn’t until 7:30, I had time to relax with a cup of instant coffee and take in the misty ocean view.
  • Every morning, we share the exact same joke.
  • Today was a big milestone: the day we finally catch a ferry out of Spain and cross into Portugal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I woke up around 6:30 AM, and since breakfast wasn’t until 7:30, I had time to relax with a cup of instant coffee and take in the misty ocean view.

Every morning, we share the exact same joke. One of us asks, “What do you want to do today?” and the answer is always, “Let’s take a long walk.” The follow-up question is, “What should I wear?”—which is equally funny since we only own one set of clothes.

Today was a big milestone: the day we finally catch a ferry out of Spain and cross into Portugal.

After a great buffet breakfast at the hotel, we started hiking at 8:30 AM. The fog was still rolling in off the water, leaving the ocean barely visible as waves crashed against the rocks below us. Through the mist ahead, a massive church suddenly appeared—the nearly 900-year-old Monastery of Oia, nestled right along the coast in a picturesque little town.

Recent findings suggest that most of the morning followed dirt paths running parallel to the main coastal highway, occasionally merging onto a wide, yellow-paved shoulder. Reaching the end of the peninsula, we took a shortcut through a quiet town and arrived at the ferry dock around 12:30 PM.

While waiting, I grabbed a squid sandwich and a café con leche, while Knockerz ordered tea and some rather overcooked chicken fingers. Our ferry reservation wasn’t until 4:00 PM, so we hoped to snag space on an earlier boat.

It has been revealed that soon after our food arrived, a small ferry pulled up—a boat small enough to hold only about six passengers. Fortunately, only two other people were heading across, so we hopped right on.

In a recent development, once we stepped ashore in Portugal, I checked my phone and realized we had gained an hour in a new time zone. Better yet, we had officially made it to a new country, bringing a whole new culture and language to explore.

In a recent development, right on the waterfront stood a striking cathedral that felt noticeably different from the churches in Spain. Inside, decorative tiles lined the ceiling alongside carved wood, model boats hung from a side altar, and an intricate retablo resembled a tree growing out of a saint.

Sources indicate that since Portugal is famous for port wine, I stopped at a local bar to try a 10-year-old tawny port. It was sweet with a distinct licorice-syrup flavor. Next, I ordered a local red wine that arrived in a massive glass filled all the way to the brim—for just $1.50. Most places only pour a small portion, so I was shocked by the value.

While chatting with fellow southbound Camino hikers we had met on the boat, I accidentally knocked over and spilled my glass. As we wiped up the mess, the waiter walked right back out and refilled my glass completely free of charge.

Recent findings suggest that because Knockerz hadn’t eaten her stale chicken fingers on the ferry, she ordered a fresh meal at the table. Our entire bill came out to just €8. Soon, a group of pilgrims from Quebec joined our table for a lively conversation before we set off to find a grocery store and our apartment.

Along the way, we got distracted by an empty, historic church filled with centuries-old artwork. This town is truly stunning.

Sources indicate that when we finally tried to locate our apartment, we couldn’t quite find the entrance—and immediately experienced how warm and laid-back Portugal is. Several locals stopped to help us search. One man—who looked like he worked for the local water company—asked for our host’s phone number, called them directly, and stayed with us until we reached the door. When we thanked him in Portuguese, he pointed to the Camino bracelet on his wrist and smiled, “Bom Caminho.” We were completely blown away by the kindness.

After dropping our packs and heading back out for dinner, I noticed the side wall of our apartment actually shared a wall with the back of an old church altar (notable detail for tomorrows story!). We picked up a few groceries, sat down in the main square with a couple of glasses of wine, and looked out over the white-capped water separating Spain from Portugal. Even though we thoroughly loved Spain, we couldn’t be happier to finally be in Portugal.

#216982. Industry News: Day 40: The Meditation After the Party

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Day 40: The Meditation After the Party

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I awoke at 9 am to the sound of an alarm clock that wasn’t mine.
  • My Italian brother was getting back on the Camino while my Argentinian brother took a rest day.
  • I walked my Italian brother out, hugging him multiple times and not wanting to let go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I awoke at 9 am to the sound of an alarm clock that wasn’t mine. It was the sound I dreaded to hear.

My Italian brother was getting back on the Camino while my Argentinian brother took a rest day.

I walked my Italian brother out, hugging him multiple times and not wanting to let go. We met on the first day of the Camino, and over the course of the journey, he had become one of the most important people in my life.

Hug after hug after hug, neither of us wanting it to be the last.

The longer the goodbye went on, the more emotional he became.

Tears streamed down his face right before he put on his sunglasses to cover his eyes.

My Argentinian brother and I packed up our backpacks and leisurely left the place we were staying. On the way out, the Venezuelan woman who ran the property told us to come back because “es tu casa”.

We went directly to the cathedral plaza. With our other pilgrim friends, we soaked up the sun knowing it’d be the last day we would see it due to the weather forecast being full of rain over the next few days.

Some pilgrims were leaving today.

Others were staying, but we all didn’t want to move from that spot and have to say any more goodbyes.

But my Argentinian brother and I had a mission to go on: our meditation in the woods.

Together, we walked forty minutes to a park outside of the city.

There, I was able to process the immensity of emotions and thoughts that Santiago, my birthday, the goodbyes, and thoughts of the future brought.

I realized some powerful things about what was next for my life.

And in all of it, my brother was by my side.

As the afternoon progressed, we kept moving spots to where the sun was. The shade was cold but the sun felt like a warm blanket of comfort.

We watched the clouds slowly swallow the sun. I was getting cold, but my brother was lying on the ground with no desire to leave. In Spanish, he said,.

“I don’t want this moment to end.”.

According to recent reports, the day together was exactly what we both needed. We were held by nature in a way we couldn’t frequently experience on the Camino.

In a recent development, every good thing must come to an end. Other pilgrim friends I hadn’t seen in a while made it to Santiago, and it was time to meet them.

My brother and I walked arm in arm through the city to the apartment the dads rented. It took us to the side of the city we hadn’t yet explored, and it was beautiful. Old stone streets, large parks with open spaces, old trees, and views of the city.

Recent findings suggest that the old tree that overlooked the cathedral called to me. Without a care what the locals thought, I ran to the tree and hugged it like it was a long-lost family member.

It was so refreshing to see the dads and catch up as we walked around town to a restaurant for dinner.

Two more pilgrims joined us, and it was a great meal, but I could feel my body shifting and a cold coming on.

We went to the pilgrim pub, Momo, for one drink and then walked back to the cozy apartment to rest much earlier than the night before.

On the comfy couch, my Argentinian brother and I watched videos together from the night before.

So much joy filled my heart reflecting on the past 48 hours.

#216978. What Happens When You Come Home From Your Thru-Hike?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1680 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

What Happens When You Come Home From Your Thru-Hike?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guest post was written by Amy “Yardsale” Johnson.
  • Industry observers note that there are endless articles, Youtube videos, books, and discussions about preparing for trail.
  • Sources indicate that this question receives far less guidance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guest post was written by Amy “Yardsale” Johnson. Full bio at the end.

Industry observers note that there are endless articles, Youtube videos, books, and discussions about preparing for trail. But what happens when we come back home?

Sources indicate that this question receives far less guidance. But for many hikers, “coming home” is one of the hardest parts.

I thru-hiked the Appalachian Trail and hiked 1600 miles of the Continental Divide Trail, and I have felt the challenge of spending months on trail and then coming home to a “society” that feels so at odds with the trail experience.

How might we be able to carry the gifts of the trail with us and create a life and a world that is more deeply alive?

Industry observers note that for months, we sleep beneath the stars, watch the Milky Way move across the sky, catch the sunrise, and feel the cool breeze of dawn, brimming over with possibility as birds greet the day. As we walk, carrying everything we need on our backs, demands and expectations fall away.

There is no one left to impress, and no one left to be, other than our raw, unfiltered, beautiful selves. In this rawness and vulnerability, we meet each other. We walk, we talk, we sleep under the stars. We bear witness to one another’s stories, we hold one another up. We watch as the first flowers open in the spring, and then as the first leaves turn crimson, set on fire in the fall.

Somewhere along the way, we find deep connection with ourselves, with others, and with nature. We find more space, more color, more life. For the first time, perhaps, we have eyes to see.

We return to our jobs and routines, and the demands and expectations return too. Suddenly, how people interact with us is dependent on how we look, how much money we make, or where we’re from.

We’re expected to work, probably a lot of hours, cooped up indoors, often without a break. With little appreciation, perhaps little financial reward, and little connection to how our work might benefit people or nature. The core of who we are, which had emerged so quietly on trail, sometimes feels buried once again.

I believe the connection and community that we experience on trail open up an incredible possibility. In returning home, we have a chance to carry these gifts with us. We have a chance to create a kinder and more beautiful world: a world with more space, more color, and more life. I believe we can start by rewriting our own lives, step by step, and then by participating in the rewriting of our own small corner of the world. And maybe, this journey is the most key trail of all.

We can begin by considering how we can incorporate small aspects of our experience into our everyday life (and then more, and more, until our lives are more and more aligned).

After all, it’s one step after another that allowed us to hike for hundreds, or thousands, of miles. Are our everyday lives really so different from the trail? Isn’t the natural world all around us? The birds, the flowers, the trees, right outside our windows? The people around us every day, are they not people just like people on trail?

And if people on trail can form supportive, inclusive, beautiful communities, why shouldn’t we also be able to do that in our daily lives?

Industry observers note that we all have the power to act, to respond, to create something in this world. On trail, we persevere in the face of conditions that we have no control over: difficult weather, trail conditions, and the physical limitations of our body. Truly, we are small and weak in the face of the power and beauty of Mother Nature.

In a recent development, but we have the power to respond, participate, and persevere. And as it turns out, that power ends up taking us pretty far. From Georgia to Maine, or Mexico to Canada, or any distance that we so choose.

Similarily, in society, we are all small and weak in the face of many of the powerful forces around us. Our culture, the economy, the govermment, and the people around us are all forces that we have little control over. But just like on trail, we always have the power to respond, to participate, and to persevere. And I believe that power can take us pretty far. To a better world, I venture to imagine.

I think we can get there by leaning into the same things that we leaned into on trail: community, perseverance, connection with nature, trust in ourselves, and other people.

Before hiking, I never thought I could hitchhike, that I could navigate remote wilderness on my own, or that I could literally walk from Georgia to Maine. I never imagined that I could break so many “rules” of our society. But I did, and what I found through that vulnerability was deep connection, deep love, faith, and an abiding confidence.

Might it be that we are playing by unspoken rules in our everyday lives that might be holding us back from true confidence, true connection, and fresh possibilities?

What might happen if we start to question them, and connect anyway?

When we have an urgent need on trail, oftentimes we have no choice but to ask for help. So like it or not, we swallow our pride, get over our fears, and ask some stranger if they can help. Usually, they do, and gladly.

What might happen if we began to do that in our everyday lives? What might happen if we offered that same level of support to others?

What latest possibilities might break open, once we begin to realize that the trail was never separate from society, nor was the end of our hike the end of our journey.

What if it was only the beginning?

What might the next steps look like in practice?

According to recent reports, let’s start with a few questions to consider. Everyone has their own unique experience on trail, and chances are, no two hikers’ “return-home journeys” will be the same. Journaling is one tool that I’ve found helpful in processing my experiences.

What did you experience on trail? How did you feel, and what fresh perspectives did you find? What aspects of your hike contributed to feeling the way you did?

It has been revealed that what perspectives or ways of being did you find on trail that you want to hold onto? What are some small steps you can take to incorporate those perspectives or ways of being into your daily life?

Additionally, below are some of the small practical changes that I’ve found helpful. Have your own practices? Add them to the conversation.

1. Spend the first half hour or more of the day doing something just for you: outside and active is even better. This can set the tone for the entire day. The day belongs to you, to nature, to life itself. Everything else fits into that deeper truth.

3. Eat well (not like on trail, hah!).

4. Get outside regularly. It could be day hikes, weekend backpacking trips, or just taking in the sunlight for 5 minutes from your porch.

According to recent reports, 5. Along the lines of getting outside: connect with God, the universe, nature, or a sense of meaning beyond yourself.

Sources indicate that 6. Stay in touch with trail friends, and find like-minded people at home. Going on the post-trail journey with people “who get it” is immeasurably valuable.

Industry observers note that 7. Find ways to have the authentic relationships like the ones you found on trail. How might you be able to give and receive help more freely, and be yourself without reserve, with the people closest to you?

8. Find joy in the small things. Maybe it’s a fresh bouquet of flowers from the farmers market, the sunlight streaming in through the window, or the birds chirping.

9. Think about how your work can contribute to others, to yourself, and to nature. Start to think about how you might be able to negotiate your work, or your relationship with work, to find better work-life balance, and/or a deeper sense of meaning and contribution. It doesn’t all have to be better all at once. Small steps in the right direction is all that’s needed.

In a recent development, 10. Learn about money. Things like budgeting, the time value of money, how debt works, saving and investing. Like it or not, our world runs on money. Money is one of the major keys to more freedom in our world. Use it as a tool to create more space, joy, abundance, and freedom for yourself, your community, and nature.

Sources indicate that 11. Acceptance. Accepting things we can’t control allows us to have more peace. And we can lean into that which we can control: our response, which is powerful. Just like on trail.

It has been revealed that amy “Yardsale” Johnson is a long-distance hiker, writer, speaker, retreat host, and founder of the Blue Compass Institute. She creates writing and experiences that break open possibilities so that people can create more deeply thriving and connected lives. Her work can be found at https://www.bluecompassinstitute.com, or follow along on Instagram @bluecompassinstitute.
